description: Our team aims to bring the stories of NASA’s equipment on the Moon and Mars to life through an interactive educational website. We want young space enthusiasts to discover the missions, hardware, and science behind these objects. We welcome teammates interested in storytelling, web development, design, space research, or education. Curiosity, collaboration, and a willingness to learn are welcome!
summary:
Project LOST SIGNAL is an interactive 3D exploration game that brings the stories of spacecraft left on the Moon and Mars to life. Players wake inside a lander, drive across planetary terrain, and use LIDAR to locate silent explorers.

Each recovery follows an engineering journey: collect metal, fabricate replacement components with an orbital station’s 3D printer, repair the spacecraft’s hardware, and troubleshoot its software to transfer mission records into a portable data drive. Oxygen limits and repair failures introduce consequences, while a final report explains the player’s successes, mistakes, and score.

The game combines NASA-sourced mission histories, authentic imagery, and spacecraft models with clearly identified fictional recovery scenarios. Available in English and Turkish, it turns learning about space exploration into an active experience. By connecting each abandoned machine to its discoveries and lasting scientific value, LOST SIGNAL encourages curiosity, problem-solving, and appreciation for the engineering behind humanity’s exploration of other worlds.
details:
Project LOST SIGNAL is a browser-based 3D educational adventure that explores the stories of spacecraft left behind on the Moon and Mars. It combines real NASA mission history with clearly identified fictional recovery scenarios, helping players understand what these machines discovered and why their scientific contributions still matter.

How it works

Players wake inside a lander and explore distinct lunar and Martian environments on foot or in a pressurized rover. A temporary LIDAR scan reveals nearby spacecraft, their identities, and distances. Each spacecraft has a briefing featuring NASA imagery, an explanation of its simulated fault, and a description of its onboard records.

Recovery follows two stages: hardware restoration and software recovery. Players collect metal salvage and travel to an orbital station, where a simulated 3D printer produces replacement components. They then return to install the parts, drag cables into their sockets, or adjust coolant valves. Once the hardware works, players read diagnostic logs and choose an appropriate software recovery action before copying records into a portable data cartridge.

Oxygen management and repair failures give decisions consequences. Running out of oxygen triggers a rescue that preserves progress but reduces the score. A final mission report explains successful repairs, lost spacecraft, recovered data, and every point deducted.

Tools and development

The project uses TypeScript, React, Three.js, HTML, CSS, and Vite. NASA mission references, photographs, and selected official 3D models support the educational content. AI assisted with coding, translation, and original illustrative scenery. Historical information is distinguished from invented faults, repair procedures, and gameplay measurements.

Creativity, benefits, and intended impact

LOST SIGNAL turns space history into an experience players participate in. Its hardware-to-software recovery sequence connects exploration with engineering, resource management, and evidence-based troubleshooting.

English and Turkish language support broadens accessibility. The project aims to encourage students and other curious players to explore NASA missions, practice problem-solving, and recognize the lasting value of spacecraft whose missions have ended.
